悬疑惊悚视觉小说游戏《审判官谢泼德》全新试玩版现已上线

news.body:
由韩国开发团队 Narrowdeep 倾力打造的悬疑惊悚视觉小说游戏《审判官谢泼德》，今日正式在 Steam 平台上线全新试玩版，游戏正式版计划于2027年推出。本次试玩版不仅对解谜与叙事节奏进行了优化，同时在原有基础上追加了简体中文字幕支持，及新增日语配音，为玩家带来极致沉浸的异端审判体验。
前往偏远之地，调查离奇古怪的异端案件
本作的故事发生在一个名为“乌克里姆”的宗教国家，玩家将化身为审判官，受命前往一座充斥着诡异流言的偏远村庄，调查一起日益猖獗的异端案件。随着调查的深入，村民谎言背后的绝望真相将逐渐浮出水面，你必须在信仰崩塌的边缘寻找一线生机。
凝视深渊的核心人物
游戏围绕多位性格迥异的角色展开，本次 Demo 中几位关键人物将悉数登场：
审判官-谢泼德： 玩家扮演的主角。身处充满敌意的环境中，你的每一次抉择都将塑造他的信念，决定他成为无情的审判官，还是探寻禁忌真相的背叛者。
可疑的向导-莉娜莉：一位开朗的自由职业导游兼纪念品手艺人，似乎对星村及其居民过分了解。
咖啡馆老板-克鲁斯：经营着“永昼”咖啡馆的中年男人，笑声震耳欲聋，但咖啡确实一流，体格彪悍得不像个咖啡馆老板。
寻找真相的审判之路
本作将文字推理、现场搜证与多分支叙事进行了完美融合：
搜证与解谜推理： 玩家需仔细搜查场景寻找物证。当调查陷入僵局，可使用主角的特殊能力“原罪粉末”强化感官，洞悉隐藏线索并击溃嫌疑人的心理防线。
充满压迫感的异端审讯： 运用收集到的情报与嫌疑人激烈对峙。你必须看穿伪装与谎言，为无辜者洗清冤屈以揪出隐藏在幕后的真凶。
抉择决定生死的审判： 审讯的最后，你必须下达“有罪”或“无罪”的最终判决。这不仅直接决定其他角色的生死，还会引发蝴蝶效应，导向截然不同的故事走向。
线下试玩亮相！确认参展2026 WePlay
《审判官谢泼德》确认参加即将于11月21-22日，在上海国家会展中心2.2馆举办的2026 WePlay活动，届时除了现场试玩外，参加对应活动，即可领取精美的周边！

游戏类型： 视觉小说 / 悬疑推理 / 心理恐怖

members.title: 小智游戏Zealory Games参展虚幻大会：以技术推动关卡与美术的无缝协作

news.body:
近日，由 Epic Games 官方主办的全球性虚幻引擎开发者技术交流盛会——Unreal Fest Shanghai 2026 在上海中心举行。作为全球虚幻引擎开发者广泛关注的行业盛会，超过2300余位来自游戏、硬件、影视动画、AI 等领域开发者与创作者齐聚一堂，围绕引擎前沿技术及项目实践展开分享与交流。
来自成都的游戏研发工作室 Zealory Games（小智游戏）受邀参加了本次盛会。工作室技术专家易恺铭发表了技术演讲，围绕“让LLM、关卡策划与关卡美术无缝协作“等内容，深度分享了项目研发与落地过程中的实践经验。
活动期间，Zealory Games 还在现场设置试玩台，邀请来自不同领域的开发者与创作者体验工作室当前在研项目《未眠野》。
为期两天的展台交流中，《未眠野》基于高度自由的物理引擎架构所实现的联机体验，引发了众多从业者的浓厚兴趣。在体验游戏的同时，不少参与者还围绕项目的前沿技术实践与玩法架构设计展开深入交流，分享各自在游戏研发过程中的技术思考与实践经验。
Zealory Games
创造极致体验
Zealory Games （小智游戏）是本次大会受邀嘉宾中的一支年轻团队，核心研发成员均来自国内一线游戏公司及其标杆项目。团队当前在研项目《未眠野》采用UE5引擎研发，持续推动技术迭代，并注重引擎技术的工程化应用，以更高效地实现游戏设计构想与品质目标。
目前，《未眠野》是Zealory Games（小智游戏）的主要在研项目，并已于9月正式首曝，迅速引发全网关注。首支宣传视频播放量迅速突破千万，并登顶B站游戏区热门榜及TAP预约榜。首曝当月，《未眠野》还开展了保密技术测试与线下试玩活动，进一步检验了产品品质与技术表现。目前，游戏全网预约量已突破百万。
作为一款基于 UE5 引擎研发的万物交互开放世界游戏，《未眠野》在画面表现上已达到一流水准，同时保持了较高的系统稳定性。在此基础上，项目团队仍在持续探索引擎技术的深度与应用边界，通过对 UE5 引擎进行深度优化与模块化重构，进一步提升物理模拟与渲染管线的性能；以扎实的技术积累，为高自由度交互玩法的稳定运行与快速迭代提供支持；并逐步构建更加高效、稳定的内容更新管线。同时，团队也将持续收集来自玩家与行业开发者的技术及体验反馈，为后续产品优化与技术迭代提供参考。
Zealory Games 团队表示，技术是推动游戏持续迭代与发展的重要动力。未来，团队将继续以《未眠野》项目为基础，分享和交流更多具有实际落地价值的技术经验，推动项目不断完善与发展。

news.title: 英伟达宣布黄仁勋辞去CEO
news.summary_raw: 英伟达董事会今天宣布，黄仁勋已辞去总裁、首席执行官及董事会成员职务，即刻生效。现任执行副总裁兼首席财务官科莱特·克雷斯已同意出任临时首席执行官。 在正式继任者确定前，克雷斯在担任临时首席执行官的同时，将继续兼任执行副总裁和首席财务官。据悉，英伟达董事会已开始寻找正式首席执行官，内部和外部人选都会考虑。此外，董事会还任命哈维·琼斯为英伟达首任董事长。 新任董事长哈维·琼斯表示，克雷斯曾协助带领英伟达实现高速增长，对英伟达的业务、客户、运营及财务状况都有深入了解。他指出，董事会对克雷斯及经验丰富的管理团队充满信心，预计英伟达的日常运营、客户承诺和产品计划都会照常推进。 克雷斯则表示，她将与管理团队一起，在黄仁勋过去33年打下的基础上继续前行。公司将继续推进让英伟达在加速计算和人工智能领域保持领先的工作，并把握未来的机遇。她强调，公司的工作重心依然是服务好客户、合作伙伴、开发者和股东。

news.title: Making the Portrait of a Harry Potter-Inspired Goblin with Realistic Skin Texture
news.summary_raw: Enrique Mateo-Sagasta talks about the challenges of hand-sculpting the exaggerated anatomy of a goblin while keeping it balanced, explains how he paints detailed, lifelike skin in ZBrush, and comments on how switching between XGen and XGen Interactive helps achieve realistic grooming.

members.title: Making the Portrait of a Harry Potter-Inspired Goblin with Realistic Skin Texture

news.body:
Making the Portrait of a Harry Potter-Inspired Goblin with Realistic Skin Texture
Enrique Mateo-Sagasta talks about the challenges of hand-sculpting the exaggerated anatomy of a goblin while keeping it balanced, explains how he paints detailed, lifelike skin in ZBrush, and comments on how switching between XGen and XGen Interactive helps achieve realistic grooming.
Introduction
My name is Enrique Mateo-Sagasta, and I'm a Senior Creature Modeler at ILM Vancouver, where I've been working for almost five years. I've worked on several shows, but Lilo & Stitch has been the most meaningful to me. I was tasked with modeling Stitch and his facial expressions. It took a lot of work, and thanks to an amazing team of talented artists, I think we were able to translate the animated character into live action pretty successfully.
It's been a busy year for personal work, too. I've become very comfortable with my workflow at home, so I've been trying to take some of my more successful studies all the way to finished pieces. That's what happened with the Chimp, the Viper, and the Goblin.
Getting Started with the Goblin
The Goblin actually started as a quick sculpt of a male bust. Once I finished, though, I thought, "Okay, another practice sculpt with no story behind it." I wanted to turn it into something more interesting, so I started gathering references.
I usually use Pinterest because one image leads to another, and the possibilities feel endless. I also tend to have movies playing in the background while I sculpt – usually films I've seen many times that still inspire me. It's almost like listening to music.
This time, I was working my way through the Harry Potter films, from the first to the last, so the Gringotts goblin influence was definitely there.
Modeling
All the main facial elements were already there in the original male bust, so the first step was to play with the proportions: larger, pointed ears, a bigger nose, and those classic goblin features. The challenge was making those changes feel believable. Even though he's a fantasy creature, the features still need to fit together in a way that makes anatomical sense. There was a lot of experimentation involved in finding that balance.
The turning point came when I focused on the size of the cranium and the relationship between the head and shoulders. Getting that relationship right established the character's sense of scale. From there, I could work my way down to the individual facial features and refine them within that overall structure.
For the wrinkles, I tried to think about the underlying anatomy and how the skin would naturally compress around the facial features. Rather than simply carving lines into the surface, I wanted the folds to have volume and direction. I use some alphas as a starting point, then build from there, adapting the finer details to the character.
The most important part is sculpting the secondary forms, such as the main wrinkles and folds, by hand, and then integrating them with the tertiary details, like pores and smaller wrinkles, so everything works together at different levels of detail. I also introduced asymmetry and smaller secondary wrinkles to make the skin feel more organic.
Topology & UVs
I usually start my sculpts from a sphere. It forces me to build the primary shapes of the head first, and I find that exercise challenging in a good way. It helps me keep those fundamental sculpting skills sharp.
Once I'm happy with the primary and secondary forms, I use a base mesh with existing UVs, provided by 3D Scan Store, and manually fit it to my sculpt. That step doesn't take me very long, although there are tools that can make the process easier.
Keeping the original UV layout allows me to use their texture maps if needed. For my personal projects, though, I enjoy painting and sculpting the details by hand, and I can work fairly quickly that way. For the Goblin, I took that hands-on approach to sculpting and skin painting.
Texturing
I find ZBrush very powerful for painting skin. I start with a base skin color and then build up regional variations, much as I would in a painting. For example, I introduce more red around the ears and nose, where blood beneath the skin can be more visible.
I use the spray functionality of the brush to introduce variation between the individual dots. That helps break up the color and adds a lot of realism. I also use a vein-shaped alpha to suggest blood vessels beneath the skin, then gradually build up more detail and variation.
Subtlety is essential, and I regularly check the results by rendering in Maya. It's easy to go too far and make the skin look painted or dirty. Being able to adjust the colors directly in ZBrush – for example, masking the lips and reducing their saturation – makes it much easier to get close to the result I want. After that, I usually only need minor adjustments during look development in Arnold.
I don't use a cavity map for the skin. I let the displacement and subsurface scattering do that work. Combined with the lighting, those elements give me the realistic skin response I'm looking for.
For the vest, I used free texture maps from Poly Haven. I use their HDRIs as well; it's a great resource and a website worth supporting. I added two fur systems to the fabric: one to break up the overall surface and another specifically for the edges. I also used Arnold's aiCurvature node to vary the diffuse appearance and give the vest a more worn look.
The shirt received a similar treatment, but its shader uses the good old tileable cloth texture built into Maya. It started as a quick shader, but the more I adjusted it, the more I liked the result. It also has a small amount of subsurface scattering, which, I think, helped. As with the vest, I used two XGen fur passes: one across the fabric and another along the edges.
When it comes to grooming the Goblin, I started in ZBrush with FiberMesh to establish the initial look. It's very simple and fast once you get used to it. Then I moved to standard XGen and finally converted everything to XGen Interactive, which gives me much more control over individual hairs. I try to take advantage of the strengths of each system, and I've found that combining all three in this order gives me the best results.
For the eyelashes, I used standard XGen, while the peach fuzz was created entirely with XGen Interactive.
Lighting & Rendering
This was an interesting part of the process. With AI assistance, I developed a tool with a simple interface that lets me switch between my HDRI maps with a click. I can rotate each HDRI, adjust its exposure, and save my favorites along with their settings.
That makes it much easier to test materials under different lighting conditions. It has also sped up look development and helped me find lighting that suits the character. For the final render in Arnold, I usually recreate the qualities I like in the chosen HDRI using Area Lights. Then I add a personal touch – perhaps an extra rim light, a change in color, or an adjustment to the intensity of individual lights.
The final images were composited in Procreate, where I added the backgrounds and some post-production details like a very subtle painted atmosphere, bloom, and chromatic aberration, enough to add a little bit more realism to the image.
Conclusion
For years, my biggest challenge has been finding a workflow that feels comfortable and allows me to work efficiently. I want to finish projects while I'm still excited about them. I have two young children and a full-time job, so my personal creative time is precious.
That's why using AI to help develop tools that speed up my workflow makes sense to me. We're at a critical moment with this technology. My approach is to use it in ways that I consider ethical and that align with my own values. It can feel intimidating for artists, especially beginners. My advice is to use it to support your development as an artist and give yourself more time for creative work. For me, the artistic decisions and the hands-on process are still the heart of it.

news.title: BioWare Co-Founder Explains the $200 Million Problem With Reviving Mass Effect
news.summary_raw: BioWare founders Greg Zeschuk and Trent Oster explain why reviving Mass Effect would require an enormous $200+ million investment—and why Canada may be better served supporting the people and institutional knowledge behind the studio.

members.title: BioWare Co-Founder Explains the $200 Million Problem With Reviving Mass Effect

news.body:
BioWare Co-Founder Explains the $200 Million Problem With Reviving Mass Effect
BioWare founders Greg Zeschuk and Trent Oster explain why reviving Mass Effect would require an enormous $200+ million investment—and why Canada may be better served supporting the people and institutional knowledge behind the studio.
In case you missed it
Our Exclusive Interview
More than 300,000 fans signed a petition begging EA to keep Mass Effect from a quiet death in its vault. Casey Hudson, who directed the original trilogy, says he’s optimistic the series will live on. The leader of Canada’s New Democratic Party wants Ottawa to help BioWare’s laid-off developers buy the studio and run it themselves. And one of BioWare's founders says he's already running the numbers on a rescue.
The outcry has been voluminous and passionate in the wake of the sudden and shocking closure of BioWare.
But bringing back the beloved studio and franchise is going to take more than heart, signatures, and a politician’s social post. It’s also going to need $200 million or more, according to two of the people who built BioWare and an industry analyst.
That may not be possible. But there’s a less expensive route that could be.
“It's nice to have these sorts of ideas, but who's going to supply the $200 million pot of money to make the game?” said BioWare co-founder Greg Zeschuk. “That's really, I think, the crux of it: Is it economically the best place for someone to invest? I know I sound harsh about it, but that's the challenge.”
BioWare
The $200 Million Question
It isn’t just Zeschuk who thinks creating the next Mass Effect would cost $200 million. Trent Oster, a member of BioWare’s founding team who co-founded the Edmonton studio Beamdog, reached the same ballpark figure.
“The scary component of Mass Effect is the audience is going to want the best of AAA development,” he wrote on Twitter on Nov. 5. “Rough ballpark (based on contemporaries) is $200M+. That is a big number to commit up front.”
I reached out to Joost van Dreunen, who teaches the business of games at NYU Stern and writes the SuperJoost Playlist newsletter, to get a sense of the numbers. He said a fully loaded developer in Canada (which would include salary, benefits, payroll taxes, equipment, and software) costs between C$125,000 and C$155,000 a year. That works out to about US$7,500 to US$9,300 a month per person.
"A Mass Effect-scale game is a different category," van Dreunen wrote. "You're looking at 200 to 300 people over five to six years, plus heavy outsourcing. That puts development alone somewhere between US$150 million and US$250 million, before a dollar is spent on marketing."
And that money covers one game, not a studio, he said.
BioWare
"To earn back US$200 million in development plus marketing, you'd need to sell around 7 million copies. BioWare has done that before, but not recently."
The last time that happened was with BioWare’s Dragon Age: Inquisition, which sold more than 12 million copies since its 2014 release. The studio’s most recent release, Dragon Age: The Veilguard reached about 1.5 million players in its launch quarter, about half of what EA was expecting.
Oster, for one, doesn't think money alone was the problem. "EA has had two, well-funded swings at making RPGs with Andromeda and Veilguard," he wrote on X on Nov. 10.
This isn’t an issue unique to BioWare, Zeschuk pointed out.
"You can look back at the last few giant releases of huge RPGs from storied studios and see they've all had challenges," he said. "You look at Starfield, you look at the original Cyberpunk, and these are great developers that are in their wheelhouse. It's super hard to do."
BioWare
That makes it an investment hard to justify from a business perspective, he said.
"Is it even worth it?” he said. “Why do I want to take this risk? And especially if I don't have this seasoned, experienced group doing it, the difficulty level just keeps going up and up."
Former Mass Effect director Casey Hudson learned that the hard way. After leaving BioWare in 2020, he started Humanoid Origin, and announced that the new studio was working on a new AAA science fiction game. It shut down in November 2024, before the game shipped, due to an “unexpected shortfall of funding.”
There are, of course, exceptions to the rule. Rockstar can spend whatever it costs to make Grand Theft Auto 6, Zeschuk said, because its return is almost guaranteed.
"Unless they can somehow magically mess it up, they'll get their money back in spades," he said. "But most other people are like, 'Oh, I'll make a new IP and take a risk.' And who knows, right?"
BioWare
What's For Sale?
Money issue aside, there’s perhaps a bigger issue facing any attempt to save the studio and game: What’s actually for sale.
When the studio closure was announced on Oct. 21 by Electronic Arts, the company wrote that it had decided “not to move forward” with the early development on the next Mass Effect. And that they would be “closing the studio and our Edmonton workspace.” About 50 BioWare employees lost their jobs, part of roughly 400 cuts across the company.
Bloomberg later reported that EA chose to fund Star Wars Battlefront 3 over the next Mass Effect while cutting costs after its $55 billion buyout by a group led by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund. An EA spokesperson told Bloomberg the decision was made "collectively" after months of review. "While this is never easy, we ultimately have to make tough decisions," the spokesperson said.
EA still owns the BioWare name and the Mass Effect and Dragon Age franchises, and a Mass Effect TV series is in development at Amazon. Asked whether it would sell or license the name or the rights, EA spokesperson Justin Higgs said the company had "no additional comments or information to share" beyond its closure note.
BioWare
Without the ability to purchase or license the franchise or studio name, “buying BioWare” really just means funding a new studio built with former BioWare staff. And Oster argued that even if you could get the rights to create a new Mass Effect, the deal would only work as part of a larger strategy.
"There has to be a bigger plan in place for the IP to make the math work," he wrote.
I asked Zeschuk if he’d have any interest in leading such an effort or would want to buy the name and the rights himself.
"No. No," he said, with little pause. "I'd love to see it continue, but I'm not the one for it. And I also don't know how. I think the challenge with it is it creates this giant web of complexity on how you execute it."
Electronic Arts
Time Costs Money
The biggest expense in game development isn’t technology: It’s time. It’s also the hardest thing to predict.
"A year of delay costs whatever the team burns in a year," van Dreunen wrote.
That means that for a 50-person studio in Canada, it would be burning through about US$4.5 million to US$5.6 million in a year. For a 250-person team, that skyrockets to US$22 million to US$28 million.
“Plus,” he added, “re-spent marketing and a year of revenue you don’t get.”
And that extra time pays for itself only when it sells enough extra copies to cover the delay, he said. At roughly US$40 net per copy, the 50-person team needs about 125,000 extra sales to break even. The bigger team needs closer to 600,000 to 700,000.
Despite that high cost, there are studios that will do exactly that, like Nintendo, Zeschuk said. The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom was delayed from 2022 to 2023, but ultimately sold 10 million copies in three days.
"They actually decided to sit on it for a year and refine it," he said, "polishing every sharp edge off it. And I'm just like, well, that's what we should be doing."
“At that scale,” van Dreunen wrote, “a year of payroll is a rounding error.”
CD PROJEKT RED
Alternatively, a studio might spend time following a game’s release fixing it. That’s what happened with CD Projekt’s Cyberpunk 2077. Despite several delays, the game shipped so broken that Sony pulled it from the PlayStation store. But years of patches and the release of the Phantom Liberty expansion ultimately saved the game, which has now sold more than 40 million copies.
"The time gets spent either way," van Dreunen wrote, "but spending it before launch protects the full-price sales window, whereas spending it post-launch means paying double to repair damaged franchise equity."
Zeschuk credits CD Projekt for sticking with it, but said most studios can't afford to take that path.
"Imagine if they had done that in the first place, but there's no way they have the time and the money," he said. "You need that period of polish. Otherwise you're just throwing something out and hoping, which is what most people do, including us at times."
Through that lens, BioWare’s Anthem can be viewed as a bit of a cautionary tale. After years of changing direction, the game was mostly built in about 12 to 16 months, according to a 2019 Kotaku investigation, and it never recovered from that launch.
BioWare
The Edmonton Problem
One of the points of saving BioWare is to keep it in its Edmonton location. But Edmonton is one of the most expensive places in Canada to try and rebuild a game studio.
Where most Canadian provinces offer refundable tax credits on game development labor, Alberta offers none. If the move were aimed at reopening the studio in Ontario, that state’s refundable tax credits would cover 35 to 40 percent of eligible spending. In Quebec it’s 30 to 37.5 percent, and in British Columbia it’s 25 percent of salaries.
"Depending on the province, you'll be able to get a tax credit on labor costs, varying anywhere from 0 percent in Alberta to 40 percent in Ontario," van Dreunen wrote. On a 50-person, four-year project, “a 40 percent credit cuts the labor bill by about a third.”

news.title: Tripwire Interactive lays off workers after announcing new publishing initiative
news.summary_raw: The Killing Floor studio lays off 36 in a move the former co-founder blames on 'woke leftists' ousting him from his position years ago.

members.title: Tripwire Interactive lays off workers after announcing new publishing initiative

news.body:
Tripwire Interactive, the Georgia-based developer and publisher behind the Killing Floor and Maneater series, has announced that the company is making 36 jobs redundant, shortly after having just announced a new publishing initiative for smaller games.
The Embracer-owned studio confirmed the layoffs on X (formerly Twitter) in a statement, reiterating that the studio is continuing work on Maneater 2 and Killing Floor 3, the latter releasing last year but struggling to match its predecessor's numbers. The news comes just days after the company announced Tripwire Presents, an initiative that scales publishing duties for smaller games. It is unclear if that initiative was announced with knowledge of impending layoffs, though Tripwire laid off 23 jobs earlier this year as part of a restructuring plan.
Tripwire co-founder and former CEO John Gibsonweighed in on this news in response to a post by game consultant Iain Garner, disagreeing with the Garner's proposed notion that Killing Floor 3 was to blame. "This wasn't the issue, it was that woke leftists got me, the CEO, key leader and creative force ousted and the company forced to be sold," Gibson said, referencing his ousting as CEO and subsequent sale to Embracer. "This narrative that CEO's are just greedy stuffed shirts is destroyed by this result. The same team that made KF3 made KF2, minus it's [sic] leader."
Gibson was the head of Tripwire Interactive until 2024, when he voiced support for Texas' anti-abortion law, leading to development partners cutting ties with Tripwire Interactive. Thus, Gibson blaming "woke leftists" for his ouster.
"I'm not saying mistakes weren't made following my departure, and I'm not saying I was the only talented person there. I lead a great team of talented individuals, and we succeeded as a team. But pull the linchpin and the machine collapses. Like kicking Steve Jobs out of Apple," Gibson added, replying to his own tweet.

news.title: How Unreal Game Adur Uses Stylized 3D Character Creator for Development
news.summary_raw: Kabengo! Games explains how its four-person team uses Character Creator 5, iClone 8, and Unreal Engine 5 to build the stylized characters, cinematics, and Basque-inspired world of Adur: Desagertzea.

members.title: How Unreal Game Adur Uses Stylized 3D Character Creator for Development

news.body:
How Unreal Game Adur Uses Stylized 3D Character Creator for Development
Kabengo! Games explains how its four-person team uses Character Creator 5, iClone 8, and Unreal Engine 5 to build the stylized characters, cinematics, and Basque-inspired world of Adur: Desagertzea.
In this showcase, Reallusion takes a look at how French indie developer Kabengo! Games uses Reallusion Character Creator 5 and iClone 8 alongside Unreal Engine 5 to produce their upcoming title, Adur: Desagertzea.
By combining CC5’s morph layer system with iClone Unreal LIVE LINK, a four-person studio achieves near-final cinematic rendering and rapid animation iteration without relying on Generative AI automation.
“I turned to Character Creator as I had been using it for a couple of years, for other various projects… and knowing its powerful features for creative efficiency. Some features I was expecting to have my hands on really impressed me, particularly ActorMixer, that we used to achieve our specific body and face proportions.”
— Paul Puaux – Creative / Artistic Director at Kabengo! Games
Featured Artist Spotlight: Kabengo! Games
For indie game developers, capturing a distinctive visual identity while maintaining production momentum is an ongoing balance. Kabengo! Games, a four-person indie studio based near Bordeaux in southwestern France, addresses this challenge directly in their debut title, Adur: Desagertzea (“Adur: The Disappearance”).
Technical Pipeline Overview
Pipeline Stage | Primary Software & Plugins | Key Technical Function / Benefit |
Character Creation & Morphing | Character Creator 5 (CC5), ActorMixer | Blends body/facial proportions to achieve stylized “puppet diorama” silhouettes. |
Shading & Texturing | CC5 Shader Engine, Overdriven SSS, SkinGen | Combines clay shaders, dynamic pores, wrinkles, and custom stencils in UE5. |
Animation & Motion Editing | iClone 8, Motion Layer Timeline, AccuFACE | Parametric facial expressions, procedural IK/FK switching, and motion editing. |
Real-Time Integration | iClone Live Link, Reallusion Auto Setup for UE5 | Streams poses and animations instantly into Unreal Engine 5 Sequencer. |
World Building & Rendering | Unreal Engine 5, Lumen, Nanite, RTX/DLSS | Real-time global illumination, high-poly geometry rendering, and cinematic post-processing. |
Interview:
Paul Puaux on Adur: Desagertzea
What inspired Adur: Desagertzea, and how does blending 2.5D exploration mechanics help you showcase Basque traditions and language?
Paul Puaux: The basic idea behind Adur: Desagertzea stems from a family anecdote in which my son nearly ran away from home one evening whilst my wife and I were gone on a night out. Gradually, the idea of turning this scenario into a game took shape.
Together with the team, we mixed and remixed the idea until it incorporated the story of our hero Adur and his grandfather Aitatxi into Basque history and mythology, set in the region where we grew up.
The team shares many common references from 1990s narrative platformers—Another World, Flashback, Heart of Darkness—and modern successors like Inside and Little Nightmares. 2D/2.5D allows us to weave narrative and gameplay together into a cinematic tapestry where the player is the hero. Basque mythology and language are cultural isolates.
This oral tradition enables us to create a world blending the ancestral and the modern—from small fishing villages to ancient forges, mountains, and the ocean.
For Adur, you needed a specific “puppet diorama” aesthetic. Why did you choose Character Creator over photorealistic options like MetaHuman Creator?
Paul Puaux: We realized early on that the storyline would be hard to build without a strong connection to our characters. The emotion they convey is essential for gameplay and cinematics. It was a no-brainer that we needed a flexible pipeline to experiment with their physical presence.
I turned to Character Creator, having used it for years across various projects. Moving to CC5 brought features like ActorMixer, which we used to achieve our specific body and face proportions. Features like overdriven Subsurface Scattering (SSS), realistic wrinkles, pores, scars, and freckles mixed with clay shaders are now regular parts of our design process.
Through the remastered Reallusion Auto Setup plugin for Unreal Engine 5, porting custom shaders turns into an exploration experience. We combine Reallusion’s built-in shading engine with Unreal’s post-processing stencils to create the stop-motion animation look of our main characters and the etched, scribbled appearance of our villains, the Beldurrak.
In that way, it shortens the path from the intention to the final render. And as time always matters in long-term projects, opting for this pipeline is a choice that’s definitely worth it.
Can you break down your animation pipeline? How does iClone LIVE LINK inside Unreal Engine 5 help a small team achieve cinematic quality so quickly?
Paul Puaux: Working in small teams on characters, world, shading, and animation is known for being a one-man band’s job. Building character reactions—whether physical or emotional—is the final gap that creates the “suspension of disbelief”.
Working with a direct link between iClone and Unreal Engine makes a massive difference. In iClone, pose and motion libraries let us quickly explore parkour-inspired movement, Basque pelota games, or caricatural moves. Multiple motion layers in a dedicated timeline allow us to edit face muscles, expressions, switch IK/FK, or correct foot sliding.
Pushing everything to Unreal Engine via Live Link allows us to adjust framing inside the final lighting setup. From there, we bake animations for our Animation Blueprints (ABP) or use Take Recorder in Sequencer while leveraging Lumen, Nanite, and RTX/DLSS hardware. This “WYSIWYG” approach lets us try 10 or 20 takes fast, pulling out the absolute best from our source material.
Pro Tip / Pipeline Hack: Using iClone LIVE LINK plugged directly into Unreal Engine 5 allows animators to test motion libraries, adjust facial expressions, and fix foot sliding in real time against final Lumen lighting and RTX shadows. This “WYSIWYG” (What You See Is What You Get) approach eliminates offline rendering delays, allowing a small studio to test 10 to 20 animation takes in the time it previously took to render one.
With your crowdfunding campaign launching soon, where can players follow your progress, and what pipeline advice do you have for other indie studios?
Paul Puaux: Our website www.kabengo.games is our central hub where the crowdfunding campaign will launch in the coming weeks. You can also follow us on YouTube, Instagram, and Facebook under Kabengo! Games, where we regularly share workflows, production logs, and behind-the-scenes updates.
Hearing Aitatxi speak Euskara to his grandson and seeing Mari appear as the mountains describe her allows players to experience this world naturally. We’re not archiving a culture; we’re handing it a controller.
My advice to solo and indie newcomers: gathering tools that fit your project is the fueling engine that keeps your world faithful to your idea. The Reallusion pipeline has been a terrific playground for building the soul of Adur, Aitatxi, and Mari. Making things memorable comes down to the moment when your characters start talking back to you in their own language.
Conclusion: Real-Time Precision Meets Cultural Storytelling
By pairing Character Creator 5 with iClone 8 and Unreal Engine 5, Kabengo! Games demonstrates how small independent teams can deliver cinematic 3D experiences anchored in regional heritage. Rather than relying on generic photorealism or unmanageable manual rigging workflows, Reallusion tools offer indie creators the artistic control needed to bring stylized characters to life efficiently.
To support Kabengo! Games and follow the development of Adur: Desagertzea, visit www.kabengo.games.

news.title: GenAI-using developers say they mostly employ it for 'research and brainstorming'
news.summary_raw: A recent survey clocked AI-generated coding as the third-most common use case for industry professionals employing generative AI.

members.title: GenAI-using developers say they mostly employ it for 'research and brainstorming'

news.body:
GenAI-using developers say they mostly employ it for 'research and brainstorming'
A recent survey clocked AI-generated coding as the third-most common use case for industry professionals employing generative AI.
What purpose does generative AI serve in game development?
That question is one developers have sought to answer since generative AI technology came onto the scene and started popping up in every tool, platform, and service with the commercial advent of large language models (LLMs) in 2022. Recently, the role of generative AI in coding has risen to the top of many of these discussions, but new data from the GDC Festival of Gaming State of the Game Industry report indicates that's not the number one use among industry professionals.
According to the report, 40 percent of industry professionals use generative AI in the workplace. Of those, 73 percent of respondants marked that "research/brainstorming" was their number one use case. 62 percent said they used it for "data analysis and summarization" and only 56 percent said they use it for "code generation/debugging." Respondents were allowed to select multiple options that described their use of the tool.
That indicates that in the world of professional game development, only half of generative AI users are using the technology to generate code.
Meanwhile 37 percent of respondents said they use the technology for game prototyping. 22 percent said they use it for "concept art and visual ideation." While some respondents said they use generative ai for content personalization or procedural generation, ultimately only six percent of player said they use the technology to create what will eventually become "player-facing content"
What forces are shaping the use of generative AI?
Adoption of generative AI tooling has been met with exceptionally fierce resistance by segments of the professional game development community, with previous data indicating that half of developers are worried that the tech may lower the quality of games. Throughout both this year's survey and reports from prior years, respondents explaining their feelings about generative AI also remain concerned over the environmental impact of AI tools and the use of copywritten material in their foundational training data.
The survey also captures sentiment from developers who say generative AI tech has enhanced their programming capabilities. This is similar to earlier comments from experts programmers like DayZ creator and Rocketwerkz creator Dean Hall have explained the tool has accelerated their ability to make games using complex programming languages and frameworks. This isn't done through "vibe coding," a practice of progressively prompting AI to make software features, but rather taking advantage of LLMs' capability to "tokenize language."
The use of generative AI to make in-game audio/visual assets or other content has been a particularly risky landmine for studios, who often have had to backpedal or alter course after unveiling said content to players.
This data from the latest edition of the State of the Game Industry report highlights how vastly adoption of and use cases for generative AI technology can vary from role to role and studio to studio. From the outside looking in, generative AI is proselytized as a tool capable of generating entire games, replacing artists, and creating fully-simulated non-playable characters, and generating entire games.
And yet the data also indicates that for game developers across many markets, disciplines, a rather different use case has started to form.

news.title: One in three developers say they've been laid off within the last two years
news.summary_raw: According to the State of the Industry survey, 34 percent of respondents have stated that they have been laid off in the last two years.

members.title: One in three developers say they've been laid off within the last two years

news.body:
In this year's State of the Industry report, an annual survey conducted by GDC Festival of Gaming, game industry professionals were asked to respond to questions concerning consistency of employment over the last two years—and some of the results are grim. One in three of those respondents, when asked if they have been laid off in the last 24 months, answered affirmatively, indicating a sharp rise since the last report. That marks 34 percent of pollees having been laid off, ballooning to 39 percent when limited just to answerers from the United States.
In the report, GDC notes that the survey results indicate a higher participation rate from people affected by layoffs, particularly in the United States.
The number of full-time employees in the United States has dropped from 59 percent last year to just 50 percent this year. At 21 percent, one-fifth report that they are currently unemployed, marking a striking 8-point increases from the previous year's 13 percent.
49 percent of respondents, rising to 55 percent in the US, reported that their companies have implemented some form of layoffs over the last year. The number seems to skew higher for those working at AAA studios, reaching 68 percent, while it decreases for workers at younger (14 percent) and older (35 percent) indie studios. Among these layoff plans, the top reasons cited were company restructuring, financial difficulties, and canceled projects.
Game workers were twice as likely to have been laid off in the past year (68 percent) than in the preceding year (32 percent). Of the respondents who said they were laid off once (79 percent), a smaller fraction reported being laid off twice (17 percent), and even less beyond that (3 percent). The largest sectors for layoffs were in quality assurance, marketing/PR, and visual and technical arts, while business operations and services were the least likely roles to face layoffs.
The churn is also slowly eroding consistency within the industry. For those that have found a new job after being laid off, only two-thirds (68 percent) are in a similar field. 28 percent of those respondents said their new job is similar to their previous one, 23 percent reporting that its better, and 17 percent stating that its worse.
9 percent state that they have left the industry altogether.
GameDeveloper.com and GDC Festival of Gaming are sibling organizations under Informa Festivals

news.title: GDC's Mark DeLoura addresses the event's dip in attendance in 2026 as he details the planned changes for 2027
news.summary_raw: The organisers of the Game Developers Conference (GDC) Festival of Gaming are not unduly phased about the 30% drop in attendance the event witnessed in 2026 .

members.title: GDC's Mark DeLoura addresses the event's dip in attendance in 2026 as he details the planned changes for 2027

news.body:
GDC's Mark DeLoura addresses the event's dip in attendance in 2026 as he details the planned changes for 2027
The VP of content strategy explains why GDC is introducing the Business Hall, how pricing has changed, and how the event is evolving with an ever-changing industry
The organisers of the Game Developers Conference (GDC) Festival of Gaming are not unduly phased about the 30% drop in attendance the event witnessed in 2026.
Speaking to GamesIndustry.biz, the event's VP of content strategy, Mark DeLoura, says that while there was a decline in the number of people at the show, he still feels that the conference is hugely valuable to the games industry.
"We always want the event to be as valuable as possible to as many people as possible," he says.
"There were still 20,000 game developers there, which was amazing. It's the biggest show for developers worldwide. Attendance was down, and that was clear to people there, but I heard people were having more substantial conversations, which was interesting. We're definitely going to try to grow the event. Our job is to make it the best possible event for as many people as we can. That's why we're making changes to try to make it more appealing. So, I suppose it is a concern, but only because there are many more game developers out there, and we need to help them, especially right now. It's our job."
GDC 2027 is undergoing some changes; the organisers have already announced that the event is being reduced to four days rather than five, "something that has been much requested," DeLoura says.
There is also going to be a new Business Hall space; DeLoura admits that a great deal of networking and business happens in the hotels and other spaces around the Moschone Centre venue, but he says that it is "incumbent" on GDC to provide an environment for these conversations to happen on-site.
"The game industry is a tough place. If we can find ways to matchmake, find ways to help people find funding, take meetings, all that sort of thing, that is our goal," he explained. "So we are going to dedicate a really large area of the show to what we call the Business Hall, and part of that will just be empty tables, meeting pods that are bookable, a big game changer lounge for executives, and lots of casual space to just hang out and take meetings. It is really the core of it."
DeLoura also says that the Business Hall is about making the event as "accessible" as possible. Passes for this section cost $125, while a Festival Hall Only pass will set attendees back $175. Academic, Indie or Startup passes are now $299, with Festival passes costing $549, down from $649. The Game Changer tier is now $1,249, a reduction from 2026's $1,699.
Another change for the 2027 edition of the show is that, in addition to the usual discipline-based tracks, there are new types of talks. The first is Hot Topic, which will focus on areas like generative AI and user-generated content. Then, as part of the pre-existing day-long GDC Summits, are the new Emerging Summits, which will also discuss new topics and change every year.
"We are just trying to be very aware of what is going on in the industry and make sure we give developers information on what is happening right now and call it out to them so it is easy for them to find," DeLoura says. "That is really the goal."

news.title: GDC State of the Game Industry report: 40% of developers are using generative AI for work
news.summary_raw: 40% of developers are using generative AI in their work, according to the latest State of the Game Industry report from the Game Developers Conference (GDC).

members.title: GDC State of the Game Industry report: 40% of developers are using generative AI for work

news.body:
GDC State of the Game Industry report: 40% of developers are using generative AI for work
Survey project lead Beth Elderkin lays bare the mood of the industry, the job market, and how people are making games
40% of developers are using generative AI in their work, according to the latest State of the Game Industry report from the Game Developers Conference (GDC).
That's an increase of 4% on the previous report, but survey project lead and content marketing manager Beth Elderkin notes that this is a smaller increase than last time.
57% of developers using the tech employ it for text generation, research, early prototyping, coding, and presentations. Generative AI is most popular with business operations and services, mobile-only studios, and free-to-play developers.
27% of AAA workers feel encouraged or pressured to use generative AI; 9% of indie developers say the same.
"People just know the technology now, and it's an actuality instead of a theoretical issue"
55% of respondents said that AI is having a negative impact on games, a 1% increase year-on-year; where previously this topic was the subject of larger percentage swings, now it has calmed down.
"What appeared to me based on the data is that the technology was not necessarily theoretical, but still early in those first two years," Elderkin tells GamesIndustry.biz.
"Last year, for the survey prior to this one, it was more part of the everyday conversation. But in this past year, it has completely changed in terms of what people know about it, how people use it, and how often people use it. So I don't know if the battle lines have been drawn. I think it's more that people just know the technology now, and it's an actuality instead of a theoretical issue, so they know how they want to use it or whether they want to use it at all."
Jobs and funding
33% of respondents have been laid off in the last 24 months, and around half said that their company had conducted layoffs. 68% of AAA staffers say that their studio has cut jobs, while 35% of respondents from more established studios have made redundancies. For younger indies, this figure is just 14%. 54% of those who have been made redundant have not found another job; 25% say they have applied for at least 100 jobs.
Looking at co-development, almost half of respondents work for studios that have used some form of external development in the last 12 months. 16% of staff at non-co-development studios say that their companies have started to offer co-development services as a means of generating extra income or diversifying their portfolio. 50% of respondents say that they had turned to self funding, often "leveraging contract work and co-development" as a means of financing their own projects.
On the funding point, Elderkin said that publishers were "expecting more" from developers before giving them financing.
"We're also seeing private equity investments start to pull back and become more reserved"
"The overall consensus was that publishers are expecting more right out of the gate," she says. "They want your game to have a high number of wishlists and a social media following, and they want it to be in a very good state. You have to get something good enough to present, but you need funding to do that. If you don't have funding, you have to figure out how to self-fund and get yourself to that point. There's also the challenge, especially for indie studios, of having more studios than available funding. We're also seeing private equity investments start to pull back and become more reserved than they were during the pandemic."
Platform trends
PC remains dominant for developers, with 81% of respondents saying they are working on their upcoming project for this platform. PlayStation 5 came in at 45%, with Xbox Series X/S at 37%.
10% of respondents are working on projects for the next PlayStation console, while 8% are developing for Xbox's upcoming Project Helix. The number of developers working on virtual reality, augmented reality, and mixed reality projects has collapsed from 8% to 3%. Asked if this is due to the changing focus of Oculus owner Meta, Elderkin says that this "could be part" of the reason why attention has dwindled.
"But I also think it's because we're not seeing many new announcements in the field. Steam is coming out with its own offering, so hopefully we'll see some growth in the future. Over the past couple of years, we've heard about VR studios shutting down, including the developers behind Moss, whose games I love. They're beautiful.
"Personally, I'm sad to see interest in VR decreasing right now, because I think there's a lot of value in that kind of immersive experience. But until we see more innovation in the space, I don't think people will focus on it. I think they've turned their attention elsewhere."
She continues: "As we see a decrease in use, we're also seeing less focus from Meta, Google, and other companies that were pursuing VR more heavily. They're moving away from it, and I think we're seeing the results. Developers don't want to make a game for a platform people aren't using or looking to expand and grow."
Game engines, crunch, and unions
Looking at engine use, Unreal and Unity came in at 35% and 28%, respectively, but were both down 7% and 2% respectively. This coincides with 23% of respondents saying that they were using a proprietary engine.
Crunch and overtime remain issues within the industry; 86% of developers say that they have worked over 40 hours in a week, with nearly half saying they needed or wanted to do this. 16% felt pressured to work longer hours. 8%, however, say they have experienced "mandatory overtime", aka crunch.
65% say that their mental health has suffered as a result of their job
63% of respondents say that this overwork could have been avoided, citing poor planning, project changes and leadership.
65% say that their mental health has suffered as a result of their job; 32% say they strongly agree that long hours and layoffs have taken a toll on their mental health.
On the topic of unionisation, 15% of US-based respondents are part of a union, a 3% increase year-on-year. 80% support unionisation within the industry, while 55% are interested in joining a union. That's a 7% drop; Elderkin initially suspected this was due to more respondents already being in unions, but in fact it was driven by an increase in respondents who were not in a union and are not interested in joining one.
For the past few years, the State of Gaming reports have made for quite stark and depressing reading. While there are still challenges to overcome, this time around, Elderkin is more optimistic about the industry looking forward.
"I think there are still a lot of challenges that are happening, and I do believe the ongoing layoffs have not contributed to a sense of stability," she says.
"One interesting statistic that we had was that folks who had been laid off sometime in the past two years and had since found another job experienced a much higher rate of job insecurity than those who had not been laid off. So there are impacts. However, one thing I am seeing this year that I didn't necessarily see in previous years is resilience, and that was really inspiring to me. We're seeing more respondents saying, 'I'm going to take it in my own hands. I'm making my own game. I'm starting my own studio.' We had a lot of students saying that in particular because they see they're entering a job market that is going to be challenging for them, so they're figuring out ways to do it themselves."
She concludes: "I'm seeing a lot of resilience and hope in the future, which was really nice to see after several years of very sad things."

news.title: "It's about giving more great games a chance" – Why Launchable thinks it can help more independent studios reach the market with its shared success model
news.summary_raw: A new platform called Launchable aims to connect studios with development talent and publishing services using a "shared-success framework". In other words, developers provide their services on the understanding that they will receive a revenue share later on, once the game launches.

members.title: "It's about giving more great games a chance" – Why Launchable thinks it can help more independent studios reach the market with its shared success model

news.body:
"It's about giving more great games a chance" – Why Launchable thinks it can help more independent studios reach the market with its shared success model
Co-CEO Greg Hall explains how the platform aims to match studios with developers, who are paid on a revenue share basis
A new platform called Launchable aims to connect studios with development talent and publishing services using a "shared-success framework". In other words, developers provide their services on the understanding that they will receive a revenue share later on, once the game launches.
Revenue share will be paid to developers for the first five years that a game generates revenue, and the terms are negotiated directly between the developer and the studio. For providing its matching service, Launchable takes a small percentage of a project's revenue.
Studios can put out calls on the platform for the specialists they need – and the idea is that the platform can help games to reach the market that would otherwise struggle to secure the necessary funding.
Launchable's co-CEO, Greg Hall, says the platform was inspired by his own personal experiences. "When I was bringing my own game to market, and later looking at projects as an angel investor, I kept meeting incredibly talented studios facing exactly the same problem; they were passionate about building their own IP, but spending a huge proportion of their time pitching for fundraising or taking on work-for-hire simply to keep the studio going, all to the detriment of their own IP projects," he tells GamesIndustry.biz.
"What struck me was how far along some of these games already were. They had great teams, playable builds and, in some cases, communities with tens of thousands of wishlists, but publishers had become increasingly risk-averse and the funding just wasn't there.
"Ultimately, it's about giving more great games a chance to make it to market."
Shared success
Hall says Launchable's shared-success model means that developers, studios, and Launchable itself all stand to benefit. "We all make money when a game launches. The more successful the game, the better we all do."
But of course, there is also a risk. If the game underperforms at launch, the development talent might receive relatively meagre compensation – and there is always the chance that the game might not make it to launch at all.
Hall says that Launchable has tried to minimise that risk by ensuring that the games on the platform have been "vetted" and are "fairly well along the way."
"Launchable sets a hurdle bar for every project we accept into our ecosystem," he says. "In addition to an evaluation of design and production documentation and team leadership, we have executive producers who approve all new entrants to the platform, ensuring we have quality projects with a strong chance for success. Additionally we will be providing service partners and other support to get the games to launch; our interest is aligned with the participants, so we are heavily invested in the success of these projects."
This kind of revenue share model isn't new: bootstrapped start-up studios, like Starship Bloopers creator Big Dumb Games, sometimes elect to pay employees via future profit or revenue share in the early stages of the company, before their first game is released and the money starts coming in. But a deferred payment model – even though it could be potentially lucrative if a game sees outsize success – won't suit everyone, given that any financial reward could be months or even years down the line.
Hall expects the platform will attract a mix of people interested in full-time, part-time, or weekend work, with some being freelance and others signing up for multiple projects. "Some studios may choose to pay their talent a full or reduced salary directly as employees and use Launchable to provide upside for successful projects," he says.
"Others will work on a full shared success model, where all of the talent's compensation will come from revenue generated by the game. We place no restrictions on studios or talent on how they choose to engage with us from a compensation standpoint." But he says the platform does mandate full transparency on expected ship dates and project status, "so that all parties have the same understanding of their arrangement."
Launch preparations
Along with Hall, the team behind Launchable includes co-CEO Andie Stokoe, chief publishing officer David Miller, and chief business officer Morten Juul.
Hall founded Reptilian Rising studio Gregarious Games in 2018, while Juul is a lawyer and dealmaker who has spent over 20 years in the games industry. Miller is a veteran of MGM, NBC Universal, THQ, Codemasters, Tencent, and Warner Bros, and Stokoe is a technology entrepreneur who has worked in energy, financial services, and fintech.
So far, Launchable has signed seven studios: Hyper Luminal Games, Bad Rhino Studios, Bossa Studios, SoKrispyMedia, Observer Interactive, Big Moxi, and Expression Games. Launchable says that it is "rapidly filling up" its closed beta phase, which is set to host a further 30 studios. These are set to be announced in early 2027.
Launchable aims to match talent with projects by asking participants to submit detailed information on their career and work preferences. "The platform then uses a combination of third party sourced verification and self-declared experiences from the talent to build a complete profile as to the skills offered," Hall explains.
"Once a studio broadcasts their need for a milestone or task, the talent matching works to find the exact person that is best suited for that role. It also provides a list of similar talent, as well as a scoring methodology that explains why each option has been proposed. The platform gives the studio and talent a visual representation of how well an applicant suits a specific role using what we call a signal map. It also allows talent to see where upskilling may improve their ability to secure new roles."
In addition to the talent-matching component, Launchable says that its platform provides "suggested deal structure" as well as "templated legal documentation" so both experts and studios can agree to "their own specific deal terms".
"Once that deal has been agreed, Launchable will crystallise and store that contract on behalf of both parties, as well as managing all downstream revenue distribution to the talent; so the talent can be confident that they will get their revenue entitlement on game launch," Hall says.
"From a studio perspective, the platform provides milestone creation and tracking functionality that allows them to see the delivery progress of each talent member in real time in the lead up to delivery. The intended result of this functionality is that a project lead using the Launchable system can easily construct, broadcast, agree and monitor all tasks involved in the next development milestone."
High bar
Launchable is aiming to work with "independent" studios, although as anyone in the industry will tell you, the meaning of this term has become vague, encompassing everything from tiny indie studios to large companies without an overall owner. But that distinction doesn't matter that much to Launchable, which welcomes both.
"Prior to our public launch, we have already secured seven studios that are either actively looking for talent or have successfully on-boarded all of their necessary additional talent via Launchable," Hall says. "We are inviting a second wave of 30 studios in the coming months on a closed-beta basis, with half of those partner studios already in discussion or committed.
"When looking at where those studios sit in terms of scale, our current closed-beta wave of partner studios spans from independent developers all the way up to AAA studios."
Launchable is also taking pains to ensure that the projects that make it onto the platform pass a certain quality bar.
"Not every project is suitable for Launchable, and not every project will be accepted onto the platform; our initial focus is on projects that are from a capable, experienced team but need some additional specialist resources to reach the finish line," Hall explains.
"Launchable can provide those resources and a framework to engage with them, without the need for substantial up-front investment. Only projects that meet the requirements of the platform will be accepted so talent should have confidence that the game is leading towards a viable launch.
"We are coming out of stealth, this is our first moment we are officially saying hello to the world, so talent can begin signing up today. We welcome talent of all sorts, from part time indies to co-dev studios between projects. Because talent can choose the projects they work on, and the length of time they work on them, we expect to have self-selected passionate believers developing these games."
The rewards for those developers could potentially be great in the long term: if a game takes off, they could see payments coming in for years after their work on the game is long finished. The model also offers a way for studios to get a game over the line in an environment where funding is incredibly hard to come by. But it hinges on whether enough "passionate believers" will be willing to bear the kind of risk that is normally borne by publishers and investors: the risk that a game might fail.

All Rights Reserved. 各位好，这里是 ApricotGame。这是《天空纪实》的第四篇开发日志。 一、设计 这一篇的核心是注意力分配：压力从多个方向同时来，NPC 各有行动，你每次只能顾一头——先管哪边，都是取舍。紧张感来自"顾不过来"，不靠堆敌人数量。 三条原则： 取舍优先：你的选择会直接影响 NPC 的处境，而不是靠火力解决一切。 NPC 不是纯负担：它们有自己的行动逻辑，需要你照看和指挥。 失败即时可读：哪边出了问题，你会立刻知道，不会莫名其妙地输。 二、美术 目标是用环境本身制造压迫感：让玩家随时觉得丛林里有东西在看着自己。 丛林要"密"：植被三层——贴地的高草蕨类、中层灌木藤蔓、高层树冠。俯视角下可通行区域被切成小块，视线被枝叶反复打断，"看不清"本身就是压力。 周边迷雾：不为好看，为减少干扰、集中注意力。 关键元素各司其职： 巨大动物骨架——地标与方位锚点，尺度对比出玩家的渺小。 断崖——NPC 活动区域，隔断它们的移动路径；崖线本身也成为玩家的视觉指引。 血水坑（待定）——平静的暗红水面泛着光，安静得反常，和四周的压迫感形成反差；它是"这里死过东西"的环境叙事。 腐烂动物尸体（待定）——颜色与姿态传达，不做过度血腥，既是环境叙事，也能吸引野兽。 色彩与光影：低饱和绿灰打底，显得潮湿、闷、旧；NPC、可交互道具、危险提示用高饱和色点缀，保证一眼找到重点。树冠在地面投下斑驳阴影，目标时隐时现，增加辨识难度。 三、背景 这片丛林是"被遗弃的猎场"——巨大骨架说明这里曾是某种大型生物的领地，如今只剩残骸。NPC 是从未来穿越回的闯入者，野兽是原住民或食腐者。 这个设定不靠大段文字交代：骨架横贯地图、水坑的分布、断崖围出的天然通道，整个场景像一张摊开的猎场残迹图，玩家自己就能拼出这里发生过什么。 原则只有一条：能被看见、摸到、走进去的设定才保留，其余只作内部参考。 欢迎加愿望单：https://store.steampowered.com/app/5246470 © ApricotGame 2026. ai.title: Introducing Gemini 4 Hydrogen

members.title: Introducing Gemini 4 Hydrogen

ai.body:
Introducing Gemini 4 Hydrogen
Today, we’re introducing Gemini 4 Hydrogen, bringing cutting-edge intelligence to everyone — with speed and efficiency for everyday coding and agentic workflows.
While our frontier models, Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Argon, excel at deep, long-horizon reasoning on your hardest problems, Hydrogen is built for rapid execution across diverse agentic workflows. With Hydrogen, we’re also bringing Gemini 4 to everyone — for all tiers of Google AI Studio, the Gemini API, Gemini for business, the Gemini app, Google Search, and paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity.
Hydrogen surpasses Argon on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its default high thinking level (51 vs. 50, and reaching 54 at its highest xhigh thinking setting), while often completing tasks faster than models in its class. Gemini 4 Hydrogen is priced flat across its entire 1 million-token context window at $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens.
Unlocking efficiencies in multi-model workloads
In real-world software development, while teams rely on frontier models like Carbon and Argon for deep architectural judgment when designing systems or untangling subtle bugs, they still need a fast, disciplined execution model for writing code, running tests, and verifying changes. Hydrogen is built to stand on its own as a model for everyday work — or to pair with Carbon and Argon as the high-efficiency execution engine in multi-model workflows.
To help make this multi-model collaboration automatic, we’re introducing Orchestrator in Google Antigravity. Rather than using a single model from start to finish, Orchestrator dynamically switches between models like Carbon and Hydrogen within the same session. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, Orchestrator reached near-Carbon task success rates while, on average, consuming 24% less quota and completing 19% faster. For workflows that require parallel agents, Carbon can act as the coordinator while Hydrogen can power worker and verifier agents to build and test changes simultaneously across isolated workspaces — helping teams ship complex projects faster without driving up token costs.
Scaling developer and enterprise workflows
Beyond multi-model workflows, Hydrogen is a major standalone upgrade for teams migrating from Gemini 3.8 Flash. It delivers significant leaps in both speed and intelligence — finishing tasks 2.5 times faster at its high default setting while more than tripling Terminal-Bench 4.1 scores (57% vs. 18.2%), cutting fabricated claims by more than 5x, and adapting cleanly when a tool call fails or a search returns empty. It also matches or outperforms competing models in its class across core developer and enterprise workflows:
- Iterative repository coding and debugging: Hydrogen handles issue resolution, debugging, rapid iteration, and codebase Q&A with focused, surgical edits — delivering cleaner, production-ready code without rewriting unrelated files. It outperforms similar-tier models on SWE-sweep where it has to discover and repair bugs without breaking existing code. To explore large repositories efficiently, the model excels at natively batching file-read and search calls in parallel rather than inspecting files one by one; in early testing across complex graphs, SQL, and data-heavy enterprise workflows, our partners have seen Hydrogen run 2x to 2.8x faster while reducing token usage by 12% to 23%, compared to 3.8 Flash.
- Open-ended agentic execution: On multi-step tasks like deep research, data analysis, and broad codebase navigation, Hydrogen ranks #5 on Agent Arena, arena.ai’s live benchmark. For deep domain reasoning and analysis, it leads its class on HLE-Diamond (58.8%), ranks #1 overall on Vals Tax Agent Bench (52.3%), ties for #1 on the Vals Legal Research Bench (55.8%), and leads its class on AutomationBench-AA.
- Multimodal knowledge work: Hydrogen pairs native 1 million-token input with up to 1 million output tokens to synthesize dense PDFs, spreadsheets, charts, audio, and recorded video into polished, cited reports and structured deliverables. It outperforms other models on the new Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark (53.4%) for end-to-end agentic knowledge work over complex visual files, and on Agents’ Last Exam v1.1 (71.6%) for end-to-end professional workflows.
- Web development: On tasks where speed matters to developers, like live UI prototyping, design-to-code iteration, and interactive app building, Hydrogen generates more functional, feature-complete layouts in fewer prompts.
Adaptable speed and intelligence across four thinking levels
We built Gemini 4 Hydrogen for real-world usability. Hydrogen’s four thinking levels — low, medium, high (default), and a new xhigh tier — offer a wide range of options across quality, latency, and cost, scaling in a smooth, predictable progression so you only wait and pay for the reasoning depth a task requires. Across thinking levels, Hydrogen matches or outperforms some of the competing models in its class while often finishing tasks faster and using fewer output tokens.
Fast, everyday help in the Gemini app and Search
For consumers, Gemini 4 Hydrogen makes it easier to get things done, staying on track and following instructions more closely across multi-turn conversations.
In the Gemini app, Hydrogen makes your everyday assistant even more helpful — it’s better at following your guidance, calling the right tools, and getting you to a reliable output with less back-and-forth.
- Ready-to-go writing, research, and everyday work: Hydrogen sticks closely to your tone, format, and specific rules, so email drafts, study guides, rewrites, and documents come back ready to use on the first try. When you are comparing products or synthesizing dense material, it pulls together clear tables and visual breakdowns without dropping key details.
- Connects the dots and gets more tasks done: Hydrogen breaks down your goal step-by-step, pulling relevant context from your uploads, Google apps like Gmail and Google Drive, and Connected Apps like Airtable and Dropbox. When you start a task in Gemini, it also more frequently calls the right tools and skills for the job, helping save you time as you check things off your to-do list.
- Everyday prototyping and iteration: For exploring and testing ideas, Hydrogen generates clean, working layouts in fewer prompts, making it easy to prototype and refine interactive projects quickly, like synthesizing real-time global lightning strike data into an interactive 3D globe.
Hydrogen is significantly upgrading Search, delivering more helpful, intuitive responses for all users globally.
- Better understands your true intent: With Hydrogen, you can ask your question in your natural flow of thought — even if you have multiple parts to your query, hard-to-understand typos, or highly specific requests — and Search will intelligently comprehend what you’re looking for.
- More visual responses: You’ll get highly adaptive, visual, and easy-to-scan responses that are uniquely relevant to your needs, at the speed you expect from Search.
- Wider range of relevant links: With Hydrogen’s advanced reasoning, we’re also upgrading our query fan-out technique in Search, connecting you to a broader range of helpful links than before, helping you find sites you previously might not have discovered.
Designed for safe, dependable execution at scale
Gemini 4 Hydrogen brings improvements from our latest Gemini 4 safety and security stack to our broadest audience yet, combining built-in training with real-time surface safeguards to help mitigate both misalignment and misuse. Beyond foundational protections, we focused on two areas that matter most for a faster model that’s for everyday work:
- Safe, aligned, and secure agentic workflows: While 3.8 Flash has strong alignment and safeguards, Hydrogen is a leap ahead. It reduces overreach in agentic tasks by up to 81% and under-service by up to 79%, and cuts misaligned actions and task shortcutting across tool-use and coding evaluations by 12x. When faced with impossible or blocked tasks, it is up to 2x less likely to bypass permission boundaries and achieves a 96.7% honesty rate on our internal agent honesty evaluation.
Building on our commitment to reasoning transparency, Hydrogen also preserves 99.9% chain-of-thought legibility with zero deceptive reasoning edits across more than 200,000 audited turns. Against indirect prompt injection attacks, Hydrogen is more than 2.3x more resilient on the Gray Swan IPI benchmark, while significantly improving robustness across tool use, computer use, and coding agents. - Helpful, reliable everyday interactions: Across our product surfaces, we tuned Hydrogen to make everyday conversations more reliable and safe. Our updated safeguards are also much more precise at distinguishing between real biosecurity risks and legitimate medical or scientific questions — keeping false refusals on HealthBench Pro under 0.4%.
For more details see the Gemini 4 Hydrogen model card.
Gemini 4 Hydrogen, available to everyone today
Starting today, Hydrogen is rolling out globally across our developer, enterprise, and consumer surfaces:
- For developers: Build with the Gemini API in AI Studio and Android Studio, try it in AI Studio and if you’re a paid Google AI Pro or Ultra subscriber, you can try it in Google Antigravity.
- For enterprises: Deploy it in Gemini for business via the API or model drop down, Google Antigravity, and in Gemini in Google Sheets for eligible business subscriptions.
- For everyone: Start using it in the Gemini app model drop down 1 and in Google Search for all users, and in Gemini in Google Sheets starting with Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers.

ai.body:
12th November 2026
Google launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen today - the lowest cost member of the Gemini 4 family.
It's actually not too far off the price of its much bigger siblings, Carbon and Argon. I'm finding Gemini 4's pricing really confusing. Here's the pricing scheme:
| Model | Dates | Input ($/M) | Cached input | Output |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gemini 4 Carbon | Through Nov 30, 2026 | $2.00 | $0.10 | $10.00 |
| From Dec 1, 2026 | $4.00 | $0.20 | $20.00 | |
| Gemini 4 Argon | Through Nov 30, 2026 | $2.00 | $0.10 | $10.00 |
| From Dec 1, 2026 | $4.00 | $0.20 | $20.00 | |
| Gemini 4 Hydrogen | $1.50 | $0.075 | $7.50 |
Carbon and Argon are the same price, and both are scheduled to double in price on December 1st. If they're the same price, why have two different models? Google says that Argon "delivers Gemini 4 intelligence with faster responses and lower token spend per turn compared to Gemini 4 Carbon" - so it may be priced the same, but it will use less tokens per task.
Hydrogen, supposedly the cheap model, is currently only a 25% discount on its more capable peers. The Hydrogen price will make more sense after December 1st, when it will represent a 75% discount. It's still considerably more expensive than Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna - they're both $0.10/$0.50, so Hydrogen is 15x that.
I had Hydrogen generate some pelicans. Here's a full comparison grid showing the pelicans for all three members of the Gemini 4 family at their three supported effort levels:
Considering how close they are in price, the difference in pelican quality for Hydrogen is quite stark.

Hydrogen is built to stand on its own as a model for everyday work — or to pair with Carbon and Argon as the high-efficiency execution engine in multi-model workflows.
Most notably, Hydrogen is the new free tier model, and is the model that will power AI features in Google Search.

members.title: “双十一”机器人在物流仓“埋头苦干”：昆腾动力开启具身智能规模化获客与交付阶段

ai.body:
“双十一”机器人在物流仓“埋头苦干”：昆腾动力开启具身智能规模化获客与交付阶段
跨境称重量方等场景完成PMF验证并出现客户复购，新一代构型机器人计划12月底发布
随着2026年“双十一”线上活动落幕，国内物流也将迎来新一波年度高峰。今年购物节周期拉长、订单波峰叠加，仓库里用工最紧张、最难补位的仍是拣货、打包、称重、量方、供包这类环节。昆腾动力的具身机器人首次进入菜鸟供应链“双十一”真实作业现场。
2026年11月，昆腾动力宣布，公司在称重量方、分拣供包、固定拣选等场景完成产品与市场匹配（PMF）验证，并在多家头部电商平台及物流企业的仓库落地，形成跨仓复制和客户复购，目前，公司已获得合计近5000台机器人的批量订单，开始进入规模化获客与交付阶段。
物流仓成了物理AI最先跑通的地方
物流仓库里，机器人面对的是持续变化：每秒前进0.3米运输线、包裹外形、包装材质、摆放姿态每一项都不同——称重、量方、换单、供包必须与输送线和业务系统衔接，完成操作后还要跟住节拍，遇到异形件、堆叠和遮挡要能自己停下来重试。
这类环节给具身智能提供了一个现实条件：单次动作的失败不会影响整条产线的生产，还可以快速获得失败反馈，系统就能及时调整重试、核验或者由人工接管，为技术迭代提供了条件。
而仓库运营方则将成功率、节拍、异常恢复、持续运营四项真实生产要求，作为判断一台机器人能否“上岗”的硬指标。
有难度、有反馈、有标准，昆腾动力把这类场景当训练场，通过真机部署回收真实物流作业数据，做深高频岗位——机器人先在真实工位上干活，交付过程本身产出数据，数据再回过来改模型。昆腾动力创始人兼CEO李强认为，具身智能的能力边界要靠足够多的真实作业撑开，而物流仓提供了高频、刚需、可核验的任务密度，正是当下技术落地所需要的。
如何在真实生产环境里追上人工效率
跨境物流是昆腾率先突破的场景。昆腾与国内一头部跨境电商平台，今年7月启动前期沟通与现场考察，随后在华东、华南推进试点，9月机器人进入仓库，10月开始签署批量采购合同。相关负责人表示，选择供应商时重点看技术准备度、对物流行业的理解，以及共同投入试点的意愿。
目前，昆腾的通用双臂机器人已完成称重、供包等岗位的部署验证，供包效率达到每小时1200件以上、成功率99%。
业务推进的速度，来自模型能力、实时作业系统与现场工程的共同进步。
模型层面，昆腾围绕视觉感知与动作策略的联合学习，提升机器人对不同包装、材质、姿态和遮挡条件的适应能力，无需新增件型就逐一编程调试。这种迁移能力直接决定下一个仓库能否更快上线。同时，为应对高动态环境，昆腾采用异步输入模型：相机、触觉与机器人本体状态按各自时序和频率进入模型，由模型学习其中的时序关系，不强制对齐。
执行层面，昆腾持续优化感知、推理与动作执行之间的衔接，把模型能力转成现场节拍，以实现从输入到指令、再到机械手臂真正运动的整条链路协同，从而把模型能力转化为连续作业能力。
迭代层面，现场的失败、人工介入和恢复过程都会进入数据闭环，团队针对高频问题做分析、后训练和回归评测，迭代以天计。这些能力为Fleet Learning体系建设提供基础，后续将进一步提高问题发现与模型迭代的自动化程度，并可复用到整个机器人集群。
系统层面，昆腾把操作策略与仓内调度、订单分配和异常处理结合，围绕整条业务流程确定机器人承担哪一段。团队此前在多设备调度上的积累让新产品更快接入现场，新一代具身系统进一步推进移动与操作的协同。
帮客户解决最重要的业务场景问题
今年9月，昆腾动力与科捷集团签署全面战略合作，联合打造物流具身智能解决方案，在科捷运营的仓库及外部客户中共同推广，首个试点项目已签约并进入实施阶段。
双方最初讨论正向拣选，现场梳理后又识别出鞋服退货上架的需求：商品检查由人工完成，机器人利用夜间非作业时段处理后续上架，缓解集中退货的用工压力。
科捷物流CTO兼仓储智能化负责人评价说：“他们不仅懂具身智能，也懂行业，能够帮助我们找到最合适的场景进行使用。”
锐太（上海）供应链总经理给出的采购标准更直接：“只要产品达到我的人效要求，我现在就可以开始采购，没有必要等待。”锐太与昆腾核心团队此前已有智能自动化项目合作，当前在退货处理、分拣和拣选场景继续探索。昆腾正在把这种需求转化为具体的产品验证与交付计划。
生态与海外：分层推进
“双十一”对物流系统是一场稳定性大考：包裹短时间快速堆积、作业节拍拉满……任何一个节点的停摆都会立即传导到整条作业线。今年昆腾机器人首次参与“双十一”大促，在真实仓储环境中承受大促订单压力，并持续运行。昆腾动力创始人兼CEO李强是原菜鸟集团CTO，在阿里巴巴体系十余年，参与建设了中国规模最大的电商物流技术体系，对于如何让“物理世界和数字世界配合解压”非常清晰，如今这套思路第一次落到机器人的大促作业现场。
与菜鸟的战略合作，方向是把菜鸟积累的仓储场景、作业经验和技术基础用于具身模型训练，并共同推进仓内机器人落地。
昆腾与顺丰也在探讨和推进分拨中心供包、仓库移动拣选等试点，并进一步探索AGV调度、包裹装笼等环节。
与此同时，昆腾动力的出海进程也在加速推进。昆腾机器人已进入菜鸟香港eHub，向全球媒体和跨境客户展示具身智能在物流场景中的应用；北美子公司成立并正在与多家北美大型零售企业签署合作协议；在韩国，昆腾与一家上市的机器人公司拟推进设立合资公司、联合开发产品。此外，在欧洲和拉美区域，昆腾也分别与本地伙伴签署合作及试点协议，建立实施、运维与客户服务能力。
从交付到真实生产力
落地场景的部署铺开，也加速了产品迭代。作为具备千台级 L4 无人车规模化运营经验的团队，通过对真实物流作业数据的采集和积累，昆核心腾团队把技术能力转化为了对真实场景所需产品的定义和标准。
据了解，昆腾动力计划于2026年12月底发布一款全新构型机器人。新产品将把真实现场积累的任务需求带进设计，围绕实际工位的作业约束展开，重点提升适用性、连续作业能力和经济性。
昆腾动力创始人兼CEO李强表示：“我们希望让每一次现场交付，都推动模型和产品再往前走一步。接下来，一方面把已经跑通的场景复制到更多仓库，另一方面把真实作业中的需求和经验带进新一代机器人。12月底我们计划发布一款全新构型的产品，让技术进展继续转化为客户可用的生产力。”
随着多场景验证、多仓复制和海外合作同步推进，昆腾动力正在把已经验证的生产价值，转成可以重复交付的产品与交付能力。机器人进入仓储生产一线，更长远的变化在于作业组织方式的变化——机器承担长期枯燥、重复、高强度甚至危险的工作，人转向更高价值的管理决策工作，同时有望缓解仓储环节长期紧张的用工压力。在人工智能与实体经济加速融合的当下，这种从真实场景中验证技术、以商业闭环反哺迭代的务实路径，正在为具身智能的规模化落地提供一个可参照的样本。

ai.summary_raw: Release: llm 0.37.2 Fixes a security issue reported by Daniel de Araujo in GHSA-v9h7-jj4g-f862 and GHSA-r639-rr7r-x72w . LLM has a mechanism called extra-openai-models.yaml - now managed by the new-in-0.37 llm openai endpoint add command - for using LLM with OpenAI-compatible API endpoints from other providers. Daniel reported two ways this could accidentally send your configured OpenAI API key to one of those providers: if the key named by api_key_name had never been stored, or if a responses: true model was run with -o chat_completions 1 . Tags: projects , security , llm , releases
ai.body:
11th November 2026
Fixes a security issue reported by Daniel de Araujo in GHSA-v9h7-jj4g-f862 and GHSA-r639-rr7r-x72w.
LLM has a mechanism called extra-openai-models.yaml - now managed by the new-in-0.37 llm openai endpoint add command - for using LLM with OpenAI-compatible API endpoints from other providers.
Daniel reported two ways this could accidentally send your configured OpenAI API key to one of those providers: if the key named by api_key_name
had never been stored, or if a responses: true
model was run with -o chat_completions 1
